ta-l1d7q2-d1e97.summary: Transitional paragraph opening the inquiry into the commonness of the power to beget, in two articles: whether the power to beget is in the Son, and whether the Son can beget.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e109.summary: First objection that the power to beget is not in the Son. The power to beget includes the character of paternity (q. 1, a. 2), and paternity is not in the Son.
claims: The power to beget includes paternity.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e112.summary: Second objection. Power implies principle, so the power to beget is the principle of generation. In no way can the Son be the principle of generation, since he would be his own principle.
claims: The Son cannot be the principle of his own generation.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e115.summary: Sed contra. The power to beget is the divine essence itself, and the Father's whole essence is in the Son.
claims: The power to beget is the divine essence, wholly present in the Son.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e119.summary: Second sed contra. No knowledge or will belongs to the Father that is not the Son's, so neither does any power, which is divided alongside them. The power to beget is in the Father, so it is in the Son too.
claims: Whatever knowledge, will, or power the Father has, the Son has.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e122.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Power of begetting' (potentia generandi) has three senses, depending on whether 'generandi' is the gerund of an impersonal verb, of a personal active verb, or of a personal passive verb. Impersonally, it is the power by which generation occurs from someone, and in this sense it is in the Son, as that by which he is begotten by the Father. Actively, it is the power to beget, which is not in the Son. Passively, it is the power to be begotten, which is in the Son, since the same power that is in the Father to beget is in the Son to be begotten. This rests on the earlier point that the power to beget is the essence, which as paternity in the Father yields active generation and as filiation in the Son yields passive generation.
claims: 'Potentia generandi' is in the Son in the impersonal and passive senses but not the active sense.
The same essence is the power to beget as paternity and the power to be begotten as filiation.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e125.summary: Reply to the first objection. As joined to its act, the power to beget includes paternity and does not belong to the Son. As rooted in the essence it does not include paternity and so belongs to the Son, in the impersonal sense: the divine essence through which generation from the Father occurs.
claims: As rooted in the essence, the power to beget belongs to the Son; as joined to the act, it does not.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e128.summary: Reply to the second objection. The power to beget is only in the Father insofar as it includes the character of principle by way of paternity, but it can be in the Son in another way, as explained.
claims: The power as principle is in the Father alone.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e131.summary: The reply to the third argument (the first sed contra) is evident from what has been said.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e134.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Will and knowledge are not principles of the Son's generation, since he proceeds by way of nature; they are principles only of creatures, produced by God like artifacts. Power, however, is a principle of the divine generation too, so it can more readily be drawn toward the personal and be proper to a person than knowledge and will can.
claims: Power, unlike knowledge and will, is a principle of the Son's generation and so can be personally appropriated.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e151.summary: First argument that the Son can beget another Son. Something can operate by a power that is not impeded, the Son has the power to beget in some way, and God's power cannot be impeded.
claims: An unimpeded power can operate.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e154.summary: Second argument. The Son is the image of the Father representing him in perfect likeness, and the Father can beget, so the Son can too; otherwise the likeness would be imperfect.
claims: The Son is the perfect likeness of the Father.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e157.summary: Third argument. An operation of a common nature found in one of its supposits is found in another, as understanding is in Socrates and Plato. Generation is an operation of the divine nature in the Father, so it is in the Son.
claims: Operations of a common nature belong to all its supposits.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e160.summary: Fourth argument. Being able to beget is a dignity of the Father, or it would not be a personal property, and there is no dignity in the Father that is not in the Son, since they are wholly equal.
claims: Father and Son are equal in every dignity.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e164.summary: Sed contra from Augustine: the least unfittingness is impossible for God. If the Son begot a Son, that Son would beget another, and so on to infinity.
claims: Even the least unfittingness is impossible for God.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e167.summary: Second sed contra. There would no longer be supreme union and equal closeness among the persons, since the divine Son would be closer to his own son than to his Father.
claims: Divine persons have equal closeness to one another.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e170.summary: Third sed contra. Whoever cannot be a father cannot beget, and the Son cannot be a father, since that would confuse the persons.
claims: The Son cannot be father without confusing the persons.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e179.summary: A further question: whether the Father can beget another Son. It seems so, since generation does not diminish his power, so whatever lets him beget one lets him beget several.
claims: Generation does not diminish the Father's power.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e188.summary: Thomas's determination on the first sub-question. Some said the Son can beget another son but the power is never actualized because of the unfittingness Augustine mentions. This is empty: in eternal things being and being able do not differ (the Philosopher), still less in God, so what is not in God cannot be there, otherwise God would be mutable. The Son simply cannot beget a son, because such a son would be in no way distinguished from the Son. Divine persons are not distinguished by division of matter, being immaterial, only by relations of origin, and one relation of origin such as filiation cannot be numerically multiplied, since that would be material multiplication. So there is only one filiation in God and therefore only one Son, and likewise only one Father. This belongs to the Son's perfection: nothing of filiation in God lies outside him, so he is the perfect Son.
claims: In eternal things, and above all in God, being and being able do not differ.
The Son cannot beget, because divine persons are distinguished only by relations of origin, which cannot be numerically multiplied.
There is only one filiation and so one Son; this is the perfection of the Son.
concepts: esse and posse in eternal things

ta-l1d7q2-d1e191.summary: Reply to the first argument. The power to beget is in the Son only as rooted in the essence, not as joined to the act of begetting, so no such act follows.
claims: The Son has the power to beget only as rooted in the essence.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e194.summary: Reply to the second argument. Wherever there is likeness there is some distinction, since likeness is the same quality in different things (Boethius); otherwise it would be identity. So perfect likeness is kept between Son and Father, who agree in all attributes with their distinction remaining. If the Son begot, the distinction between Father and Son would vanish, since they are distinguished only by relations of origin and there can be only one paternity.
claims: Likeness requires distinction; the Son's perfect likeness to the Father includes their distinction.
If the Son begot, the distinction between Father and Son would collapse.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e197.summary: Reply to the third argument. Begetting is an act of the divine nature only insofar as the divine nature is paternity, and under that aspect the nature is not in the Son.
claims: Begetting belongs to the divine nature only as it is paternity.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e201.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Dignity is predicated absolutely, so Father and Son have numerically the same dignity, as they have the same essence. As paternity in the Father is the essence, and the same essence is in the Son not as paternity but as filiation, so the numerically same dignity is paternity in the Father and filiation in the Son.
claims: Father and Son share numerically one dignity, which is paternity in the Father and filiation in the Son.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e211.summary: Reply to the further question. There cannot be several sons in God, not because the Father's power is lacking but because the distinction of supposits in the divine nature would be destroyed.
claims: The Father cannot beget another Son, not from lack of power but because the distinction of supposits requires a single filiation.

ta-l1d7q2-d1e221.summary: An expositio textus on Augustine's remark that divine generation would be immoderate if the begotten Son begot a grandson for the Father. An objection holds that endless generation would be the greatest good, each generation being infinitely good. Thomas gives three unfittingnesses. (1) An infinite process would leave divine generation never complete, since every infinite is imperfect. (2) There could be no distinction among several begotten. (3) Communication belongs to nature's nobility, but infinite communication comes from a defect of nature, which, unable to preserve itself eternally in one individual, preserves the species by an endless succession, which does not fit God at all. On 'it was not that he could not, but that it was not fitting': the reading seems forced, but 'non potuit' can be taken as mere negation (as the objection did) or quasi-privatively as an infinite term, and 'non enim non potuit' denies incapacity. Against the inference that the Son is impotent if he cannot beget, as Augustine argued for the Father: begetting belongs to the very notion of a father, so any lack there would be the Father's impotence, but begetting does not belong to the notion of son and is even opposed to filiation. One is impotent only in what pertains to oneself.
claims: An infinite series of divine generations would be imperfect, indistinguishable, and a mark of natural defect.
The Son's not begetting is no impotence, since begetting is opposed to filiation.
One is called impotent only for failing in what pertains to one's own nature.

ta-l1d7q2-Dd1e146.summary: Sub-question 1 states arguments that the Son can beget another Son: from his unimpeded power, his perfect likeness to the Father, the commonness of the nature's operations, and the equality of dignity. Sed contra arguments cite Augustine's infinite regress, the persons' equal closeness, and the confusion of persons.

ta-l1d7q2-Dd1e174.summary: Sub-question 2 asks whether the Father can beget another Son, given that generation does not diminish his power.

ta-l1d7q2-Dd1e183.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 1 holds that the Son simply cannot beget. In God being and being able do not differ, and the persons are distinguished only by relations of origin, which cannot be numerically multiplied, so there is only one filiation and one Son. This unicity is the Son's perfection. The replies note that the Son has the power only as rooted in the essence. Perfect likeness includes distinction, which a begetting Son would destroy. Begetting belongs to the nature only as paternity, and Father and Son share numerically one dignity, which is paternity in one and filiation in the other.
claims: The Son cannot beget; there is only one filiation and one Son.
Being and being able are identical in God.

ta-l1d7q2-Dd1e206.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 2 holds that the Father cannot beget another Son. This is not from any lack of power but because several sons would destroy the distinction of supposits in the divine nature.
claims: The Father cannot beget another Son, not from lack of power but because it is impossible.

ta-l1d7q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 2 announces two articles on the commonness of the power to beget: whether it is in the Son and whether the Son can beget.

ta-l1d7q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 asks whether the power to beget is in the Son. Thomas distinguishes three senses of 'potentia generandi' according to the gerund: impersonal (the power by which generation occurs), active (to beget), and passive (to be begotten). The power is in the Son in the first and third senses, but not the second, since the same essence is the power of active generation as paternity and of passive generation as filiation. Power, unlike knowledge and will, can be drawn toward the personal because it is a principle of the generation itself.
claims: The power to beget is in the Son impersonally and passively, but not actively.

ta-l1d7q2-Dd1e138.summary: Article 2 asks whether the Son can beget, and in a further sub-question whether the Father can beget another Son. Both are denied. Persons are distinguished only by relations of origin, which cannot be numerically multiplied, so there is one paternity, one filiation, one Father, and one Son. In God being and being able do not differ, so no unexercised power to beget exists. The impossibility reflects the distinction of supposits, not a lack of power, and the Son's perfect likeness to the Father includes the distinction that a begetting Son would erase.
claims: Neither can the Son beget nor the Father beget another Son.
Divine persons are distinguished only by unmultipliable relations of origin.

ta-l1d7q2-Dd1e216.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 7 explains why endless divine generation would be unfitting: it would be imperfect, would leave the begotten indistinguishable, and would mark the natural defect that species perpetuation remedies. It interprets 'not that he could not, but that it was not fitting' and shows that the Son's not begetting is no impotence, since begetting is opposed to filiation.
claims: Infinite divine generation would be imperfect and a mark of natural defect.
The Son's not begetting is not impotence.

ta-l1d7q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 7 treats the commonness of the power to beget. Article 1 shows, by distinguishing impersonal, active, and passive senses of the gerund 'generandi', that the power is in the Son as the power by which he is begotten, but not as power to beget. The one essence is the active power as paternity in the Father and the passive power as filiation in the Son. Article 2 denies that the Son can beget or that the Father can beget another Son. Persons are distinguished only by relations of origin, which cannot be multiplied, and in God being and being able coincide, so the impossibility reflects the structure of the divine persons, not any lack of power. The Expositio explains why an infinite series of generations would be unfitting and why the Son's not begetting is no impotence.
claims: The power to beget is in the Son only in the impersonal and passive senses.
There can be only one Father and one Son, since relations of origin cannot be multiplied.
The Son's not begetting is not impotence, because begetting is opposed to filiation.
